chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
title: Practicing with Oswald Gibson and his first arranging: Song of India
summary: He and the young saxophonist put together a four-piece Tommy Dorsey-style Song of India, which Malachi sees as his first arranging.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Anyway, we made it through the summer. And this kid and I became fast friends, the saxophone player... He was studying with somebody down at the Marine Barracks here in Washington, studying clarinet and saxophone. So in the mornings he would be up early practicing. I forget the name of this book that he had, that he was practicing out of. It was a very popular saxophone or clarinet book. Because I've seen a lot of clarinet players with it. He would sit up, and he'd be running the exercise...
Yeah. So I would go down to the piano. So what would happen was, after we both had practiced singly for a while, we'd begin to get together.

Around that time, Tommy Dorsey had this arrangement on "The Song Of India" that was very popular. And I think this was my first association with arranging. In this group, we had four pieces. We had piano, drums, trumpet, and of course, the saxophone player who played clarinet too. He and I sat down, and I gave him the notes to play on his clarinet. Then the trumpet player, we'd tell him certain notes to play, and we'd wind up playing something separately that sounded like Tommy Dorsey, which was a big hit in the club. And the fact that I had put it all together, I felt like I had really done some arranging there! I didn't know what it was then, but it was putting it together... Because then I didn't even know anything about what an arrangement was. It was just the idea that I had this thing, and I showed it to the clarinet player, showed him the right notes, which was really nothing but chromatic (da-da/da-da-da)... Anyway, that went well, and we both learned quite a bit.
